frames.narration: Table doctors holds alice (on_call=1, xmin=10) and bob (on_call=1, xmin=10). Rule: at least one stays on call. Tx 11 and Tx 12 begin at the same time. Each snapshot sees every commit up to Tx 10.
Both run SELECT count(*) WHERE on_call. Both read the same version of each row and both get 2. Nobody took a lock.
Tx 11 sees 2, so it is safe to leave: UPDATE alice SET on_call=0. This writes a new version (xmin=11) and stamps the old one xmax=11. Tx 12 still sees the old version.
Tx 12 also saw 2, so it runs UPDATE bob SET on_call=0. Different row, so no write-write conflict and no waiting.
Both commit under snapshot isolation. First-committer-wins finds no overlapping row, so both succeed. Now zero doctors are on call. This is write skew.
Replay at SERIALIZABLE. The checker records that Tx 11 read bob (which Tx 12 writes) and Tx 12 read alice (which Tx 11 writes). Each depends on the other: a cycle.
Tx 11 tries to commit with both an incoming and an outgoing dependency. It is aborted (SQLSTATE 40001). Tx 12 then commits, so exactly one doctor is off call.
The app retries Tx 11 with a new snapshot. It now counts 1 on call (alice alone), so the rule check fails and Alice stays on call. The rule holds, at the price of one retry.

Dead versions remain: bob v1 (xmax=12) is invisible to everyone newer than Tx 12. Vacuum can reclaim it once no snapshot older than 12 is still open. A transaction left idle since before Tx 11 would pin it, and every later dead version, on disk.
